english.notes: See H9072 for the conspiracy of this offence. There is no attempt version of this offence as such a charge is not considered to be appropriate. The substantive offence is completed once a representation is made (with the requisite intent). It is immaterial whether the fraud is ultimately successful. (i) A representation is false if it is untrue or misleading, and the person making it knows that it is, or might be, untrue or misleading (section 2(2) of the Fraud Act 2006).(ii) Representation means any representation as to fact or law, including representation as to the state of mind of the person making the representation or any other person (section 2(3) of the Act).(iii) A representation may be express or implied. Meaning it could be made in words or communicated by conduct. It could be written, spoken, posted on a website etc. or implied by conduct, for example by tendering a credit card a person represents that he has authority to use if for that transaction. This would also cover so-called 'phishing', where large numbers of emails are sent to people representing that they have been sent by a legitimate financial institution (section 2(4) of the Act).(iv) A representation may be regarded as made if it (or anything implied in it) is submitted in any form to any system or device designed to receive, convey or respond to communications (with or without human intervention). Meaning fraud can be committed where a person makes a representation to a machine and a response is produced without the involvement of a human being, for example by using a 'CHIP and PIN machine'. (Section 2(5) of the Act.)(v) The test for dishonesty in all criminal cases is that established in the case of Ivey v Genting Casinos (UK) Ltd (trading as Crockfords) 2017, as confirmed in R v Barton and another 2020.(vi) The offence requires an intention of making a gain or causing loss or risk of loss; the gain or loss does not actually have to take place.(vii) Fraud can also be committed by failing to disclose information, section 3 of the Act and H8686, and by abuse of position, section 4 of the Act and H8687.(viii) Section 12 of the Act makes provision for directors, managers, secretaries or other similar officers or person purporting to act in such a capacity to be liable to prosecution where a body corporate has committed this offence.(ix) When formulating charges different considerations must be made to those applied to crime recording (applying the Home Office Counting Rules).

other.penalty:
Either way
Summary: maximum 6 / 12 months imprisonment and / or fine.
Indictment: maximum 10 years imprisonment and / or a fine.

The maximum penalty on summary conviction is 6 months for offences committed before 2nd May 2022; for offences committed on or after that date it may be 6 or 12 months depending on the general limit in a magistrates’ court, see section 1(3) of the Fraud Act 2006 and section 224(1) and (1A) of the Sentencing Act 2020.

On the 12th March 2015 the limit on fines imposed by a Magistrates' court was removed – as such, the potential fine on summary conviction in relation to an offence committed after this date is unlimited.
